name: Financial-Modelling_Version_1
summary: This repository is an AI-assisted financial modelling tool. You enter a company name, and the app researches it, asks questions, picks comparable companies and typical industry assumptions, then builds a five-year set of financial statements (income statement, cash flow, balance sheet) and a company valuation. Results can be viewed on web pages and exported to Excel. The code looks like it is mid-transition: there are older single-file scripts at the top level, a newer structured backend and a React frontend, and several parts (PDF export, the calculation route, the model wizard page, most Excel tabs) are still placeholders.
who_its_for: People who want a quick first-draft financial model of a company, such as analysts, students or founders. A developer would be needed to set it up and finish the unfinished parts.
how_it_runs: It is designed to run as containers (backend on port 8000, frontend on port 5173, plus an Ollama AI model server and Redis) started with docker-compose, or installed locally with install.sh. AI features use either a local Ollama model or OpenAI, chosen in settings or in the .env file.

areas.name: backend/calc
areas.summary: The math engine. Separate files handle revenue, cost of goods, operating costs, capital spending, debt, working capital, taxes, and valuation, and statements.py joins them into the three statements. It also includes sensitivity testing.
areas.why: This is where the actual numbers in a model come from.
areas.debug_tips: If a figure looks wrong, find the file for that line item and check its inputs first. If the balance sheet does not balance, start with statements.py.

areas.name: backend/api
areas.summary: The web routes the frontend calls: models, scenarios, defaults, research, agents, settings, export and the step-by-step workflow. The calculation route currently returns fixed placeholder numbers, and PDF export is a placeholder.
areas.why: It connects what users see on screen to the calculations, AI agents and database.
areas.debug_tips: Check the route file matching the feature that fails. If calculation results never change, that is expected until the placeholder is replaced.

areas.name: (root files)
areas.summary: Top-level files: setup and run files (install.sh, docker-compose.yml, .env.example, requirements.txt) plus older stand-alone code (financial_modeling_core.py, excel_exporter_enhanced.py, app_backend.py, Simple_Standalone_Example.py).
areas.why: They set up the project, and the older scripts appear to be an earlier version of the same idea.
areas.debug_tips: For install or startup problems, check these setup files first. It is unclear which older scripts are still used by the newer backend.

areas.name: backend/agents
areas.summary: The AI helpers. Each handles one job: researching, finding comparable companies, asking questions, building the model or reasoning about choices. The orchestrator runs them in order, and base.py sends the actual prompts to Ollama or OpenAI.
areas.why: They provide the AI-driven part of the product.
areas.debug_tips: If AI replies fail or are empty, check base.py and the provider settings in config.py. Research.py needs a Tavily key to search the web. reasoning.py was only partly visible, so its state is unclear.

areas.name: frontend
areas.summary: Configuration for the React web app: package list, build settings, styling setup, TypeScript rules and a Dockerfile.
areas.why: It defines how the user interface is built and served.
areas.debug_tips: If the screen will not load, check package.json and vite.config.ts, and confirm the port 5173 is reachable.

areas.name: frontend/src
areas.summary: The actual screens: a navigation bar, a Dashboard listing saved models, a Settings page for choosing the AI provider, and a placeholder model wizard page.
areas.why: This is what users see and click.
areas.debug_tips: If a page is blank or shows no models, check that the backend is running and answering. The wizard page is intentionally empty.

areas.name: backend
areas.summary: The backend's own setup files: main.py starts the server and connects all routes, config.py reads settings, plus the Dockerfile, requirements and project settings.
areas.why: Nothing in the backend works unless these start correctly.
areas.debug_tips: For startup errors, read main.py and config.py, and check that the .env values are present.

areas.name: backend/research
areas.summary: Helpers that fetch and tidy outside data, mainly Aswath Damodaran's industry betas and risk premiums, with disk caching, citations and field cleanup.
areas.why: It supplies market data that feeds assumptions such as the cost of capital.
areas.debug_tips: If research data is stale or missing, check the cache files and whether the Damodaran website download worked.

areas.name: static
areas.summary: Plain web pages served directly by the backend. index.html (named ORACLE) takes a company name and shows a built model. The others are older or backup versions.
areas.why: They give a simple interface that works without the React frontend.
areas.debug_tips: If the page does not show results, check the browser's error messages and that the backend route it calls responds. Which page is the main one is not fully clear.

areas.name: backend/db
areas.summary: Database setup and the definition of every table, covering models, scenarios, drivers, segments, inputs, calculated results and research data.
areas.why: It is how models and results are saved between visits.
areas.debug_tips: If saving or loading fails, check database.py for the connection and models.py for the table layout. The database type used is not stated in the summaries.

areas.name: backend/defaults
areas.summary: Typical starting assumptions for ten business types, such as SaaS and Retail.
areas.why: It gives users sensible starting numbers instead of a blank form.
areas.debug_tips: If an industry gives odd defaults, look in industry_defaults.py. Only part of the file was reviewed, so the lookup functions are unclear.

areas.name: Everything else
areas.summary: No files were assigned to this group.

readiness.summary: Top three fixes: add sign-in or an API key check since the backend is open to anyone, add real automated tests (only an empty `backend/tests/__init__.py` exists), and set up database migrations with a backup plan. After that, scan git history for secrets and pin and audit dependencies.

checks.question: Does the app build and start with one documented command?
checks.evidence: `README.md` documents a multi-step start (install Ollama, pull models, `pip install -r requirements.txt`, copy `.env.example`, `python main.py`), and `docker-compose.yml` plus Dockerfiles exist. It is not one command, and the build was not run.
checks.next_step: Add a single documented command such as `docker compose up` and confirm it works.

checks.question: Are there automated tests, and do they pass?
checks.evidence: Not checked: tests were not run in this pass. Only one test file is tracked (`backend/tests/__init__.py`), which is empty of real tests as far as shown.
checks.next_step: Add real tests for the financial calculations (DCF, 3-statement) and run them in CI.

checks.question: When something goes wrong, does the app show a clear message instead of crashing or failing silently?
checks.evidence: Not checked: error handling in the source was not inspected. The scan found 0 swallowed errors, but that does not show that users get clear messages.
checks.next_step: Review API endpoints and the UI for clear error responses when Ollama, OpenAI or Tavily fail.

checks.question: Does it check what people type or upload before using it?
checks.evidence: Only 2 input validation matches in 2 files were found, which is thin for an app that takes financial assumptions and possibly uploads.
checks.next_step: Add schema validation (for example pydantic models with ranges) on all API inputs and file uploads.

checks.question: Are passwords and API keys kept out of the code and out of git history?
checks.evidence: `.env.example` is the only tracked env file, `.gitignore` mentions `.env`, and 0 secret-looking strings were found at HEAD. Git history was not scanned.
checks.next_step: Run a history scan (gitleaks or trufflehog) to confirm no keys were ever committed.

checks.question: Can only the right people see and change things (sign-in and permissions)?
checks.evidence: 0 auth, session or permission matches in 0 files. Anyone who can reach the backend on port 8000 can use it, including spending the OpenAI and Tavily keys.
checks.next_step: Add sign-in or at least an API key check before any public deployment.

checks.question: Is important data backed up, and are database changes made through migrations?
checks.evidence: No migrations folders found, even though `alembic` and `sqlalchemy` are listed in `requirements.txt`. No backup process is documented in the evidence.
checks.next_step: Run `alembic init`, create an initial migration, and document a backup routine for the database.

checks.question: Are third-party packages reasonably up to date and free of known security problems?
checks.evidence: Not checked: the dependency audit was not run. Packages in `requirements.txt` use open lower bounds (`>=`) with no pinned lockfile for Python, so builds may not be reproducible.
checks.next_step: Pin versions, remove unused heavy packages (jupyter, seaborn if unused) and run `pip-audit`.

checks.question: If it breaks while people use it, will logs or alerts show what happened?
checks.evidence: Only 3 logging matches in 2 files. The README mentions real-time agent logging, but no error tracking or alerting is evident.
checks.next_step: Use structured logging with levels across the backend and add error alerting (for example Sentry).

checks.question: Does it stay fast with realistic amounts of data and users?
checks.evidence: Not checked: no load or performance testing evidence, and the code was not profiled. LLM calls to local models are likely slow.
checks.next_step: Measure response times for a typical model run and add timeouts and background jobs for long AI calls.

checks.question: Is there a written, repeatable way to deploy it and to roll back a bad release?
checks.evidence: `DEPLOYMENT.md`, `backend/Dockerfile`, `frontend/Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` exist. No CI config is present and rollback steps are not shown.
checks.next_step: Add a CI workflow and a short rollback section (tag images, redeploy the previous tag) to `DEPLOYMENT.md`.

checks.question: Could someone new run it and understand it from the docs alone?
checks.evidence: Many docs exist (`README.md`, `SETUP.md`, `START_HERE.md`, `DEPLOYMENT.md` and others), and the README quick start is clear. There are too many overlapping files, which may contradict each other.
checks.next_step: Consolidate into one README with a single setup path and move the rest to a `docs/` folder or delete stale ones.

readiness.method: Static evidence only; tests, build and audit were not run in this pass.

steps: Confirm a .env file exists, copied from .env.example.
Read the startup logs for the first error.
Check that the database setup in backend/db/database.py succeeds.

debug_playbook.symptom: AI features return errors or nothing
steps: Check which provider is selected, Ollama or OpenAI.
If OpenAI, confirm the key is set; if Ollama, confirm its container is running.
Try the Settings page to switch providers and retry.
Note that the calculation route returns fixed placeholder numbers.
Compare with the real math in backend/calc to see what is not yet connected.
Ask a developer to wire the route to the calc files.

debug_playbook.symptom: Balance sheet does not balance or a figure looks wrong
steps: Find which line item looks off and open its calc file.
Check the inputs it received, such as growth or tax rate.
Review how statements.py combines it into the balance check.
Check that the backend is running on port 8000.
Open the browser's developer console for failed requests.
Test the models route directly to see if it returns data.

glossary.meaning: Linked income statement, cash flow statement and balance sheet.
Discounted cash flow, a way to value a company by bringing future cash back to today's value.
Weighted average cost of capital, the rate used to discount future cash.
The estimated value of the company beyond the forecast years.
Money tied up in customer bills, stock and supplier bills.
Spending on long-lived assets like equipment.
Rerunning the model with different inputs to see how results change.
A piece of code that asks an AI model to do one specific job.
A tool that runs AI models on your own computer.
Similar public companies used as a yardstick.
